summary: This document describes a simple way to encapsulate SCTP packets in UDP packets, and its limitations. This lets SCTP work across legacy NATs that do not support it. It also lets applications implement SCTP without direct IP-layer access or special privileges.

plainLanguage.summary: This document shows how to wrap an SCTP packet inside a UDP datagram. That gets SCTP through firewalls and NAT devices that only understand UDP, and lets an application use SCTP without special privileges.

subtitle: Carries SCTP packets inside UDP datagrams so SCTP can cross networks and firewalls that do not know SCTP.

tldr.problem: SCTP normally runs directly over IP, so it cannot cross a legacy NAT or firewall that does not handle it, and it is hard to run from an ordinary application without special privileges.
tldr.mechanism: The document puts a UDP header between the IP header and the SCTP common header, uses the UDP port 9899 on both ends, and defines how ports, checksums, path MTU and embedded addresses must be handled.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from May 2013, updated by RFC 8899, and it lets SCTP work through UDP-only paths without giving up SCTP's reliability and congestion control.

today: RFC 6951 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2013. It is updated by RFC 8899 and has not been obsoleted, so UDP port 9899 remains the assigned port for encapsulated SCTP.

sections.title: Why Put SCTP Inside UDP
sections.content:
SCTP, as defined in RFC 4960, runs directly over IPv4 or IPv6. The document gives two main reasons for encapsulating SCTP packets into UDP packets. The first is to let SCTP traffic pass through legacy NATs, which do not provide native SCTP support as specified in the NAT behaviour documents. The second is to let SCTP be implemented on hosts that do not give direct access to the IP layer, so that an application can use its own SCTP implementation where the operating system does not provide one.

Nothing is lost by the wrapping, because SCTP itself provides the congestion control and the reliability service that UDP does not perform. The document also notes that the scope is limited: it covers SCTP endpoints dealing with legacy constraints and does not cover generic tunnelling endpoints. The exit strategy is to use hosts that support SCTP natively and middleboxes that support SCTP as specified.
sections.plainLanguage: SCTP normally talks straight to the network. Wrapping it in UDP lets it travel over paths that only understand UDP, and the reliability and congestion control still come from SCTP itself.

sections.title: Two Use Cases in Detail
sections.content:
The first use case is a portable SCTP implementation. Some operating systems support SCTP natively. For others, implementations exist but need special privileges to install or use, and in some cases no kernel implementation is available at all. Most operating systems require special privileges to access the IP layer directly from a user process. UDP encapsulation makes it possible to provide an SCTP implementation as part of a user process with no special privileges at all.

One point matters for an implementation in user space: the source address of outgoing packets needs to be controlled. That is not an issue if the SCTP stack can use all the addresses configured at the IP layer as source addresses, but it is an issue when the address management required for NAT traversal is also in use.

The second use case is legacy NAT traversal. For single-homed associations, IP addresses MUST NOT be listed in the INIT and INIT-ACK chunks. To use multiple addresses, the dynamic address reconfiguration extension (RFC 5061) MUST be used only with wildcard addresses in the ASCONF chunks, in combination with RFC 4895. For multihomed associations, the address management described later in the document MUST be performed. SCTP sends periodic HEARTBEAT chunks on all idle paths, and those can keep the NAT state alive.
sections.plainLanguage: Two situations benefit. A program that cannot touch the network layer can still speak SCTP. And a connection through an old NAT works, as long as the addresses inside the SCTP packet are left as placeholders.

sections.title: Ports and Associations
sections.content:
UDP-encapsulated SCTP is normally communicated between SCTP stacks using the IANA-assigned UDP port number 9899, named sctp-tunneling, on both ends. Other ports may be used in some circumstances: an implementation in the application space might be required to use ports other than the registered one, and because NAT devices may change UDP port numbers, the receiver might observe port numbers other than those the sender used. Discovering alternate ports is out of scope, but the section sets out considerations for SCTP stack design in light of their possible use.

Each SCTP stack uses a single local UDP encapsulation port number as the destination port for all its incoming SCTP packets. The uniqueness of that local port is not required by the protocol, but it greatly simplifies implementation, since a different port for each address would require the sender to choose the right port while doing source address selection. A single local port per host is not possible when the SCTP stack is implemented as part of each application, several applications are in use, and some of them want the same IP address.

An implementation that supports UDP encapsulation MUST maintain a remote UDP encapsulation port number per destination address for each SCTP association. Because the remote stack may use ports other than the well-known port, each port may differ from stack to stack, and because NAT devices remap ports, the remote ports for different remote IP addresses may differ even when they belong to the same stack. Implementations need to allow other port numbers to be set as local or remote UDP encapsulation ports through APIs.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends normally listen on UDP port 9899. Each stack keeps one local port and remembers the port to use for each remote address of each connection.

sections.title: The Packet Format
sections.content:
To encapsulate an SCTP packet, a UDP header as defined in RFC 768 is inserted between the IP header as defined in RFC 791 and the SCTP common header as defined in RFC 4960. The IPv4 version of the format is the IPv4 header, then the UDP header, then the SCTP common header, then the SCTP chunks.

The IPv6 version adds the IPv6 base header and any number of IPv6 extension headers, where the number m of extension headers can be zero, before the same UDP header, SCTP common header and chunks.
sections.plainLanguage: There is nothing clever about the format. A UDP header is simply slotted in between the network header and the SCTP header, and the rest of the SCTP packet follows unchanged.

sections.title: Encapsulating and Decapsulating
sections.content:
Within the UDP header, the source port MUST be the local UDP encapsulation port number of the SCTP stack, and the destination port MUST be the remote UDP encapsulation port number maintained for the association and the destination address to which the packet is sent. Because the SCTP packet is the UDP payload, the length of the UDP packet MUST be the length of the SCTP packet plus the size of the UDP header.

The SCTP checksum MUST be computed for IPv4 and IPv6, and the UDP checksum SHOULD be computed for both. Although UDP with a zero checksum over IPv6 is allowed under certain constraints in RFC 6936, this document does not specify mechanisms for that mode: deployed support may be limited, and at the time of writing a zero UDP checksum would run against the goal of legacy NAT traversal.

On receipt, the UDP header is removed and the generic lookup an SCTP stack performs whenever a packet arrives is used to find the association for the received SCTP packet. After finding the association, which includes checking the verification tag, the UDP source port MUST be stored as the encapsulation port for the destination address the SCTP packet was received from. When a non-encapsulated SCTP packet is received by the stack, the encapsulation of outgoing packets belonging to the same association and the corresponding destination address MUST be disabled.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending means adding a UDP header with the right ports and length. Receiving means taking that header off, finding which connection the packet belongs to, and remembering the port it came from.

sections.title: ICMP, Path MTU, Addresses and ECN
sections.content:
When an ICMP or ICMPv6 response arrives, there may not be enough bytes in the payload to identify the SCTP association the triggering packet belonged to. If such a packet cannot be related to a specific association, or the verification tag cannot be verified, it MUST be discarded silently. In particular the SCTP stack MUST NOT rely on receiving ICMP or ICMPv6 messages, and implementation constraints could prevent processing them. Where they are processed, an ICMP message of type Destination Unreachable with code Port Unreachable SHOULD be treated as one with code Protocol Unreachable, and an ICMPv6 message of type Destination Unreachable with code Port Unreachable SHOULD be treated as one of type Parameter Problem with code unrecognized Next Header type encountered.

For the path MTU, an endpoint that starts encapsulating the packets of a path MUST decrease the path MTU of that path by the size of the UDP header, and if it stops encapsulating them it SHOULD increase the path MTU by the size of the UDP header. When performing path MTU discovery as described in RFC 4820 and RFC 4821, it MUST be taken into account that the feedback from ICMP or ICMPv6 cannot be relied on. If the implementation does not allow control of the Don't Fragment bit in the IPv4 header, path MTU discovery cannot be used and an implementation-specific value should be used instead.

When UDP encapsulation is used for legacy NAT traversal, IP addresses that might require translation MUST NOT be put into any SCTP packet. A multihomed association is therefore set up initially as a single-homed one, and RFC 5061 in combination with RFC 4895 adds the other addresses. Only wildcard addresses go into the SCTP packet. When addresses change during the life of an association, RFC 5061 MUST be used with wildcard addresses only, and an endpoint that receives an ABORT with the T-bit set MAY treat that as an indication that the addresses seen by the peer might have changed.

Finally, if the implementation supports sending and receiving the ECN bits for the IP protocols in use, those bits MUST NOT be changed during sending and receiving.
sections.plainLanguage: Four details catch people out. Error messages cannot be relied on. The maximum packet size shrinks by the size of the UDP header. Real addresses must not go inside the SCTP packet. And the congestion signals must not be tampered with.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Encapsulating SCTP into UDP adds no security considerations beyond those already given in RFC 4960 and RFC 5061. Firewalls that inspect SCTP packets must also be aware of the encapsulation and apply the corresponding rules to the encapsulated packets.

One attack is described. An attacker might send a malicious UDP packet towards an SCTP endpoint to change the encapsulation port for a single remote address of a particular association. As specified in the decapsulation procedure, this requires the use of one of the two negotiated verification tags, which protects against blind attackers in the same way as described in RFC 4960 for SCTP over IPv4 or IPv6. Non-blind attackers can affect an SCTP association using UDP encapsulation in the same way as they can affect associations that do not use it.
sections.plainLanguage: The wrapping adds no new weaknesses of its own. Firewalls need to know about it, and an attacker who tries to redirect a connection still has to get the verification tag right.
